Database storage and crash recovery

Follow a stock update from memory to storage and see how PostgreSQL recovers after an unexpected shutdown.

Data pages and memory buffers

PostgreSQL organizes table and index data into pages. When a query needs a page, PostgreSQL can use a copy already in shared buffers or load the page if needed. A changed page in memory is called dirty until it is written out.

-- Run twice and compare shared buffer hits and reads.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT title
FROM courses
WHERE id = 1;

Write-ahead log and checkpoints

A dirty page can still be in memory when a transaction commits. How can PostgreSQL recover the stock update if the server loses power before that page is written? PostgreSQL records page changes in write-ahead log (WAL) before the corresponding changed data pages reach durable storage. With normal durability settings, it flushes the required WAL before confirming a commit. It can write the data pages later.

-- PostgreSQL: compare these statistics before and after a write.
SELECT wal_records, wal_bytes
FROM pg_stat_wal;

SELECT num_timed, num_requested
FROM pg_stat_checkpointer;
Checkpoint
Writes dirty pages as part of establishing a recovery point. Recovery can start replaying WAL from the redo point associated with the checkpoint.
Crash recovery
If the server stops after confirming a stock update but before writing its data page, recovery can replay the logged change on startup.

When a restore is needed

WAL replay can recover after a crash when the server still has the data files and WAL it needs. Restoring a deleted record or recovering from storage loss needs another source for the data. Crash recovery brings a database with intact storage back to a consistent state. For accidental deletion or storage loss, use a tested backup and restore procedure. Point-in-time recovery requires an appropriate base backup and the archived WAL needed to reach the target time.

# Restore a custom-format backup into a separate test database.
createdb learning_restore
pg_restore --exit-on-error -d learning_restore learning_db.dump

# Verify the restored course data.
psql -d learning_restore -c "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM courses;"
